blocks.text: 1. Query Expansion

blocks.alt: An original query gets synonyms and related terms added to become an expanded query

blocks.text: Query expansion, covering how a query itself can be enriched before retrieval runs, shifts attention from the document side to the query side.
It adds related terms or phrasings to a query before searching with it.
2. Shifting Focus To The Query Itself
Every topic so far improved how chunks get stored or ranked.
Query expansion instead improves the query being searched with in the first place.
3. Why A Short Query Often Underperforms

blocks.alt: A short query like python error misses rich context

blocks.text: A short, vague query produces an embedding with less specific signal.
That thin signal can retrieve a broader, less precise set of chunks.
4. Adding Synonyms And Related Terms

blocks.alt: The term car adds synonyms automobile and vehicle

blocks.text: Appending synonyms or closely related terms to a query gives it more surface area to match against.
A query about login problems also benefits from including terms like authentication or sign in.
5. Expanding With An LLM

blocks.alt: An original query goes through an LLM to produce expanded terms

blocks.text: A language model can generate plausible related terms or phrasings automatically.
This replaces manual synonym lists with dynamic, context aware expansion.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Expansion method","Flexibility"],"rows":[["Manual synonym list","Static, needs manual maintenance"],["LLM based expansion","Dynamic, adapts to query context"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Expanding For Both Dense And Sparse Retrieval

blocks.alt: An expanded query feeds both dense retrieval and sparse retrieval

blocks.text: As with the one dimension per vocabulary term structure in Sparse Retrieval, expanded terms help sparse retrieval find exact matches it would have otherwise missed.
Expanded phrasing also shifts a dense embedding toward more relevant meaning, since similar meaning means nearby points in vector space.
7. The Risk Of Over Expansion

blocks.alt: Too many added terms cause the query meaning to drift

blocks.text: Adding too many loosely related terms can dilute a query's original, focused intent.
An over expanded query can start retrieving chunks about only tangentially related topics.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Expanding a focused query like "reset password" with loosely related terms like "account" and "settings" can pull in unrelated results about account settings that have nothing to do with password resets.

blocks.text: 8. Latency Cost Of Expansion
Generating expansions, especially with an LLM, adds an extra processing step before retrieval even starts.
That added latency has to be weighed against the retrieval quality gained.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Calling a language model to expand every single query adds real response time before retrieval even begins, a cost that needs to be justified by a measurable improvement in retrieval quality.
{"headers":["Expansion approach","Latency impact"],"rows":[["Static synonym lookup","Minimal added latency"],["LLM based expansion","Noticeable added latency per query"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Query Expansion Is Worth Applying

blocks.alt: Short or ambiguous queries being common points toward query expansion

blocks.text: Short, ambiguous, or underspecified queries benefit most from expansion.
Already detailed, well specified queries, by contrast, gain little from further expansion.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Expanding a query so aggressively that it dilutes the original, focused search intent.
Using static synonym lists instead of considering more flexible, context aware LLM based expansion.
Ignoring the added latency cost that query expansion introduces before retrieval even starts.
Applying expansion uniformly to every query instead of only those that actually need it.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Query expansion adds related terms or phrasings to a query before retrieval runs.
It improves the query itself, unlike earlier topics that improved chunks or ranking.
A short, vague query produces an embedding with less specific retrieval signal.
Appending synonyms or related terms gives a query more surface area to match against.
A language model can generate dynamic, context aware expansions instead of static synonym lists.
Expanded terms help both sparse retrieval's exact matching and dense retrieval's semantic matching.
Over expansion can dilute a query's original intent and pull in tangentially related results.
Generating expansions adds real latency that must be weighed against retrieval quality gained.
